exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```haskell
main :: IO ()
main = print (zip [1, 2, 3] "ab")
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `zip` does not pad: it stops as soon as either list runs out.

hints: A string is a list of characters.
`zip` stops at the end of the shorter list.
exercises.solution: `"ab"` is the list `['a', 'b']`. `zip` pairs elements until either list ends, so the `3` has no partner and is dropped: `[(1,'a'),(2,'b')]`. Characters are shown in single quotes.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```haskell
main :: IO ()
main = print [x * y | x <- [1, 2], y <- [10, 20]]
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Two generators combine every `x` with every `y`, like nested loops; they do not pair them up like `zip`.
Not yet. A comprehension keeps duplicates: 2 × 10 and 1 × 20 both give 20.

exercises.solution: The generators act like nested loops with `y` inside: `1*10, 1*20, 2*10, 2*20`, which is `[10,20,20,40]`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```haskell
main :: IO ()
main = print (foldr (\x acc -> x - acc) 0 [10, 4, 1])
```

feedback.message: Not yet. That is what a left fold, `((0 - 10) - 4) - 1`, would give. `foldr` nests to the right.
Not yet. Work from the innermost parentheses outwards: `10 - (4 - (1 - 0))`.

hints: Replace each `:` in `10 : 4 : 1 : []` by the function and `[]` by `0`.
exercises.solution: `foldr f 0 [10, 4, 1]` is `f 10 (f 4 (f 1 0))` = `10 - (4 - (1 - 0))` = `10 - (4 - 1)` = `10 - 3` = `7`. With `foldl` the same subtraction would nest the other way and give -15.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```haskell
main :: IO ()
main = print (sum [x | x <- [1 .. 20], x `mod` 3 == 0])
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `[1 .. 20]` stops at 20, so 21 is not included.

hints: List the multiples of 3 from 1 to 20.
exercises.solution: The comprehension keeps 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18, whose sum is 63. The same thing with `filter` is ``sum (filter (\x -> x `mod` 3 == 0) [1 .. 20])``.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```haskell
main :: IO ()
main = print (scanl (+) 100 [-30, 50, -20])
```

feedback.message: Almost. `scanl` includes the starting value as the first element.
Not yet. That is what `foldl` would return; `scanl` keeps every intermediate result.

hints: `scanl` returns the initial value followed by each running total.
exercises.solution: Starting from 100: 100, then 100 − 30 = 70, then 70 + 50 = 120, then 120 − 20 = 100. `scanl` returns all of them: `[100,70,120,100]`. Its last element is always what `foldl` would have returned.

exercises.prompt: Which of these expressions finish evaluating, given that `[1 ..]` is infinite? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `foldr (\x acc -> x > 10 || acc) False [1 ..]`
options.feedback: Yes. When `x` reaches 11, `||` returns `True` without looking at `acc`, so the rest of the list is never needed.

options.label: `foldl' (+) 0 [1 ..]`
options.feedback: Not yet. A left fold must reach the end of the list before it can return, and this list has no end.

options.label: `take 3 (map (* 2) [1 ..])`
options.feedback: Yes. `map` produces elements on demand, and `take 3` asks for only three.

options.label: `length (filter even [1 ..])`
options.feedback: Not yet. `length` must count every element, and there are infinitely many even numbers.

hints: Laziness lets a computation stop early only if nothing forces it to look at the whole list.
Which of these functions must see the end of the list before answering?
exercises.solution: (a) and (c) finish: `foldr` with a short-circuiting function, and `take` on a lazily produced list, look at only a finite prefix. (b) and (d) must consume the entire list to produce their answer, so they run forever.

exercises.prompt: A colleague builds a list of 100,000 results with `foldl' (\acc x -> acc ++ [f x]) [] xs` and finds it very slow. Why, and what is the usual fix?

options.label: `++` copies its whole left argument, so each step costs time proportional to the list built so far; use `map f xs` (or build with `:` and reverse once).
options.feedback: Yes. The total cost grows with the square of the length. `map f xs` builds the list in a single pass.

options.label: `foldl'` is slow; use plain `foldl`.
options.feedback: Not yet. The fold is not the problem, and plain `foldl` would add laziness problems of its own.

options.label: Lists cannot hold 100,000 elements efficiently; use a `String`.
options.feedback: Not yet. A `String` is itself a list (of characters), and lists of that size are fine.

hints: How much work does `xs ++ ys` do, as a function of the length of `xs`?
exercises.solution: `acc ++ [y]` walks and copies all of `acc` to attach one element at the end, so building n elements costs about n²/2 steps. Here the whole fold is just `map f xs`, which conses each result onto the front in one pass. When you truly need to accumulate, prepend with `:` and `reverse` once at the end.
